title: Height-one quotients associated to invariant restricted tangent subalgebras
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], with an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All group schemes are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smooth and connected mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Tori and groups of multiplicative type have the meanings of [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type]. For a smooth group $J$, write $\mathfrak j=T_{J/k,e}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], with bracket induced by commutators [def-wf-lie-algebra]; $\operatorname{Ad}$ is the differential of conjugation. Fix a faithful closed linear representation of $J$ into $\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group]. A tangent vector is semisimple if its matrix in this representation is diagonalizable over $\bar k$, and is central if its bracket with every tangent vector is zero. Nilpotent for a group means that it has a finite descending central series of closed normal subgroup schemes with commutators lowering the series. In characteristic $p>0$, $X^{[p]}$ denotes the tangent vector whose left invariant derivation on $k[J]$ is the $p$-fold composite of the derivation of $X$. A restricted Lie subalgebra means a $k$-linear subspace closed under brackets and $X\mapsto X^{[p]}$. A homomorphism is finite faithfully flat when its coordinate algebra is a finite faithfully flat module over the target coordinate algebra; a finite group scheme is infinitesimal if its coordinate algebra is local with nilpotent augmentation ideal. Radicial means universally injective on geometric points. Assume $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, let $J$ be smooth and connected, and let $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak j$ be a restricted Lie subalgebra stable under the adjoint action as a group-scheme representation. There exist a finite normal infinitesimal subgroup scheme $H\subseteq J$, with $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\mathfrak h$, and a smooth connected affine group $Q$ of finite type, together with a finite faithfully flat radicial quotient homomorphism $q:J\to Q$ with $\ker q=H$ and $\ker(dq)=\mathfrak h$. The subgroup $H$ has height at most one: in its coordinate algebra each element of the augmentation ideal has $p$th power zero. One has $\dim Q=\dim J$ for Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. If the adjoint action on $\mathfrak h$ is trivial and every element of $\bar k\otimes_k\mathfrak h$ is semisimple, then $H$ is central in $J$ and of multiplicative type. Here central means that $H(A)$ commutes with $J(A)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. The case $\mathfrak h=0$, $H=1$, $q=\operatorname{id}_J$ is allowed.

source.place: Propositions 11.35--11.37 and Corollary 11.38, printed pp.222--223 (height-one subgroup correspondence and quotient); Proposition 17.80 proof, p.378, for its toral central specialization. The central multiplicative-kernel clause spells out the height-one subgroup attached to a trivial-adjoint toral restricted subalgebra.

proof.text: Apply restricted rational differentiation to $J$: invariant derivations give the restricted Lie identities and the stated tangent bracket. A tangent derivation of $k[J]$ is determined by its values on finitely many algebra generators, so $\mathfrak j$ embeds linearly in $k^N$ for some finite $N$. The given subspace $\mathfrak h$ therefore inherits a finite-dimensional restricted Lie algebra. Apply height-one integration to $\mathfrak h$ and its inclusion into $\mathfrak j$. It gives $H=\mathcal G(\mathfrak h)$ and a closed immersion $i:H\hookrightarrow J$ whose differential is this inclusion under $\eta_{\mathfrak h}$. In particular $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\mathfrak h$. The integration theorem gives finiteness, locality of $k[H]$, and $a^p=0$ in its augmentation ideal, If $a_1,\ldots,a_m$ is a basis of the augmentation ideal, then every monomial of degree greater than $m(p-1)$ contains an $a_i^p$, hence is zero. The augmentation ideal is therefore nilpotent, so $H$ has all the asserted infinitesimal and height properties.

source.place: Propositions 11.35--11.37, pp.222--223; Corollary 11.38, first sentence of proof.

proof.text: Check normality on arbitrary test algebras, rather than just field-valued points. For a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in J(A)$, adjoint stability gives an invertible restricted Lie map $a_g:\mathfrak h_A\to\mathfrak h_A$: conjugation preserves invariant derivations, commutators and $p$th compositions. The relative Hom bijection integrates it to $b_g:H_A\to H_A$; integrating $a_{g^{-1}}$ and using uniqueness shows that $b_g$ is an automorphism. The maps $c_g\circ i_A$ and $i_A\circ b_g$ from $H_A$ to $J_A$ have equal differential, namely $\operatorname{Ad}(g)\circ di_A$. Uniqueness in the same bijection makes them equal. Consequently conjugation preserves $H(A')$ after every $A$-algebra extension $A'$, proving that $H$ is a normal subgroup scheme.

source.place: Corollary 11.38, p.223: adjoint stability implies normality; relative Hom uniqueness spells out the scheme-theoretic argument.

proof.text: The affine normal-quotient theorem now represents $Q=J/H$ by an affine finite-type group, with a faithfully flat finitely presented homomorphism $q:J\to Q$, scheme-theoretic kernel $H$, and torsor isomorphism $J\times_kH\simeq J\times_QJ$. It also makes $Q$ smooth, since $J$ is smooth. The surjective continuous map $|J|\to|Q|$ makes $Q$ connected: a nontrivial clopen partition of $Q$ would pull back to one of $J$. To prove finiteness of $q$, base change it along itself. The torsor isomorphism identifies this base change with the projection $J\times H\to J$, which is finite: its coordinate algebra is a free $k[J]$-module on any finite $k$-basis of $k[H]$. The map $q$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact (between affine schemes). Finiteness descends along this fpqc cover by the cited finiteness-descent theorem. Thus $q$ is finite faithfully flat.

source.place: Corollary 11.38, p.223; quotient and torsor geometry in Propositions 5.24--5.29, pp.104--105; finiteness descent: Stacks Tag 02LA, descent.tex, lemma-descending-property-finite.

proof.text: For every algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$, $H(\Omega)=\{1\}$: a coordinate map $k[H]\to\Omega$ kills its augmentation ideal since its elements have $p$th power zero. If $x,y\in J(\Omega)$ have the same image under $q$, then $x^{-1}y\in H(\Omega)$, so $x=y$. This is precisely radiciality as defined in the item. For tangent vectors use $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$: a vector of $\operatorname{Lie}(J)$ killed by $dq$ is exactly a dual-number point at the identity lying in the scheme-theoretic kernel $H$. Hence $\ker(dq)=di(\operatorname{Lie}(H))=\mathfrak h$. Finally both group schemes are nonempty by their identity sections, and finite type; $q$ is finite and surjective. The finite-surjective dimension theorem gives $\dim Q=\dim J$.

source.place: Corollary 11.38, p.223, tangent kernel; finite-surjective dimension: Stacks Tags 00OK and 00OY as stated by lem-sc-finite-surjective-dimension.

proof.text: Suppose now that the adjoint action on $\mathfrak h$ is trivial. In the construction of step 2 one has $a_g=\operatorname{id}$ for every test algebra $A$ and $g\in J(A)$. Relative Hom uniqueness gives $b_g=\operatorname{id}_{H_A}$ and hence $c_g\circ i_A=i_A$. Evaluating on any $h\in H(A)$ gives $ghg^{-1}=h$. This proves centrality with its required quantification over all commutative $k$-algebras, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Corollary 11.38, p.223, relative uniqueness; central specialization used in Proposition 17.80, p.378.

proof.text: Put $F=\bar k$ and restrict the differential of the given faithful representation to $\mathfrak h_F$, acting on $F^n$. The trivial adjoint action implies $[X,Y]=0$ for $X,Y\in\mathfrak h_F$: differentiating $\operatorname{Ad}(1+tY)(X)=X$ gives $[Y,X]=0$. The differentiation theorem identifies this bracket with the matrix commutator. Thus the matrices for a finite basis $X_1,\ldots,X_r$ of $\mathfrak h_F$ commute. Each is diagonalizable by the geometric semisimplicity hypothesis. For a diagonalizable matrix $T$, in an eigenbasis the equation $(T-\lambda)^Nv=0$ forces each coordinate of weight different from $\lambda$ to vanish, since its coefficient $(\mu-\lambda)^N$ is invertible. Its generalized $\lambda$-eigenspace is therefore its ordinary eigenspace, and their sum is $F^n$. Apply the joint-generalized-eigenspace theorem to this finite family: the common ordinary eigenspaces span $F^n$. Extracting a basis from their spanning eigenvectors gives one basis in which every $X_i$, and therefore every element of $\mathfrak h_F$, is diagonal. The argument includes $r=0$.

source.place: Proposition 17.80, p.378, toral specialization; joint-eigenspace theorem: Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Eigenspace/Pi.lean:194--201.

proof.text: Let $T=\mathbf G_{m,F}^n\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,F}$ be the diagonal torus in that basis, so its tangent space consists of diagonal matrices and its restricted operation is matrix $p$th power (this follows by differentiating multiplication of units). The differential of the given representation now yields a restricted Lie map $\mathfrak h_F\to\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. Integration and its field-extension compatibility give $f:H_F\to T$ with this differential. The composite $H_F\xrightarrow fT\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{n,F}$ and the original closed immersion $H_F\hookrightarrow J_F\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{n,F}$ have the same differential. The integration Hom bijection over $F$ makes them equal. The surjection $F[\operatorname{GL}_n]\to F[H_F]$ of this closed immersion factors through $F[T]$, so $F[T]\to F[H_F]$ is surjective as well; hence $f$ is a closed immersion. This is the definition of $H$ being of multiplicative type: over $\bar k$ it is a closed subgroup of a split torus.

source.place: Propositions 11.35--11.37, pp.222--223, and Proposition 17.80, p.378; closed-subgroup definition of multiplicative type, Section 12.14, p.236.

proof.text: If $\mathfrak h=0$, then its restricted enveloping algebra is $k$, its finite dual is $k$, and $\mathcal G(0)=1$. Taking $Q=J$ and $q=\operatorname{id}_J$ gives the stated zero case; all kernel, height and dimension assertions reduce to their definitions.

source.place: Propositions 11.35--11.37, pp.222--223, applied to the zero restricted Lie algebra.

proof_origin.place: Corollary 11.38, p.223, expanded via Propositions 11.35--11.37; explicit relative-Hom and geometric toral arguments for the central multiplicative-type clause of the Q77 statement; Proposition 17.80, p.378.
